3eee006664:
This chapter covers three things. How to decide whether retrieval is needed at all. How to turn a messy document estate into an index that returns the right passage for the right person. And how to keep that index correct as the sources change.

It builds the whole pipeline from first principles:

  • parsing to typed elements;
  • chunking along the structure authors already wrote;
  • metadata and access control on every chunk;
  • contextual retrieval and embeddings;
  • a vector index next to a lexical one;
  • idempotent updates, freshness and revocation, and migration.

Telecom contracts, network runbooks, rate tables and retail policy documents carry the examples. You also get a from-scratch Python pipeline (chunkers, BM25, a toy embedder, contextual prefixing, ACL-aware index, re-ingestion) and a Java/Spring AI analogue.
42ede59bdc:
Reading time: 3.5 to 4 hours  ·  Companion code, 18 runnable Python examples plus a Java program for this chapter: ccarp-companion/08-rag-pipeline-design/ (run bash run_all.sh; every example works offline with --mock).

The corpus, the embedder, and every price, latency and accuracy figure in the examples are synthetic or illustrative planning numbers. Before a number goes into an ADR, check the docs for current model names, prices, cache multipliers, minimum cacheable lengths and database options.

Retrieval strategies and ranking are chapter 9. Evaluation method and statistics are chapter 11. Exam facts for CCAR-P (item count, domain weights) come from third-party summaries of the published blueprint, so verify them against the official exam guide.
4f35ab8c94:
Retrieval-augmented generation is a data pipeline whose output is a searchable index, and almost every failure that looks like a model problem is an ingestion or indexing fault: the right passage was never retrieved, it was retrieved without the context that gave it meaning, or it was retrieved for a person who should not have seen it.

Build the smallest pipeline that clears the numbers on the requirements card, cut documents along the boundaries their authors already drew, put identity and freshness into the index itself rather than into the prompt, and keep a change only when a labelled query set says it helped.
3e245eb9b9:
Everything in this chapter follows from those two sentences.

The model at the end of a RAG system is the part you can swap with one line of configuration. The index is different. It encodes your documents, your permissions and your update process, and it is hard to change once a million chunks sit in it.

That asymmetry is why the blueprint puts this topic under Integration rather than under prompting. It is also why exam scenarios about RAG rarely have a model-capacity answer. The answer is about the data: whether to retrieve at all, what the unit of retrieval is, what metadata rides with each unit, where the access filter runs, and how the index stays correct tomorrow.
927e362055:
The blueprint for Domain 3 (Integration, 19 percent) names this topic directly: evaluate RAG pipeline chunking and indexing, and match the retrieval design to the data shape and query pattern.

Three neighbouring domains reach into it:

  • Domain 5 (Governance, Safety and Risk) asks that retrieval never surface what the caller may not see. So access control is an indexing decision.
  • Domain 4 (Evaluation, Testing and Optimization) asks that every change be measured. So this chapter treats chunking and enrichment as experiments with a table of results.
  • Domain 1 (Solution Design) supplies the first question: is RAG the simplest architecture that works?

Other chapters own the rest. Chapter 9 covers the query side: hybrid search, fusion, reranking and the accuracy against latency trade-off. Chapter 11 covers evaluation method. Chapter 7 covers identity propagation, and chapter 5 covers the prompt caching mechanics this chapter uses for cost arithmetic. Where a topic belongs to one of those chapters, this one says "see chapter N" and moves on.
86480948ab:
CCAR-P does not ask which parameter sets the chunk size. It asks questions like this one. A legal team has 40,000 contracts. Answers cite the wrong clause 18 percent of the time, and the pipeline uses fixed 1,000-token chunks. What is the first change?

To answer it, you need to understand why fixed windows cut clauses in half and merge unrelated sections. You also need to know what a structure-aware splitter and a section path do about it.

So the chapter builds every stage from first principles. It runs each design choice against a small synthetic corpus in the companion folder, and it puts numbers on the trade-offs. That way you can reason about a scenario you have never seen.
0f6553c60b: Retrieval-augmented generation looks new, but each component has a lineage. Knowing it tells you which old lessons apply (most of them) and which are new (a few, mostly about cost and context).
b48a19658a:
Gerard Salton's SMART system at Cornell in the 1960s represented documents and queries as vectors of term weights. It ranked documents by cosine similarity. That is the vector space model, and it predates neural embeddings by half a century.

Karen Spärck Jones proposed inverse document frequency in 1972. The idea: a term that appears in few documents tells you more than one that appears in all of them. Put term frequency and inverse document frequency together and you get TF-IDF.

The practical machinery to serve it was the inverted index, a map from each term to the list of documents that contain it. Every lexical search engine still works this way.
c4ec50cda8:
The refinement that matters for this chapter came from the Okapi system of Stephen Robertson and colleagues, evaluated at the TREC conferences in the early 1990s. BM25 adds two ideas to TF-IDF. First, term frequency saturates: the tenth occurrence of a word adds much less than the second. Second, a document's score is normalised by its length relative to the average. Section 16 implements it in a dozen lines.

Apache Lucene, released by Doug Cutting in 1999, packaged the inverted index for general use. Elasticsearch (2010) and OpenSearch then wrapped Lucene in a distributed service. Lucene's default scoring moved from TF-IDF to BM25 around 2016.

When this chapter says "the lexical index", it means this lineage. It is the reason a part number or an alarm code can be found exactly: the inverted index treats it as a single rare term.
eb4c575419:
Lexical matching cannot find a document that says "terminate" when the query says "cancel". Latent semantic indexing (Deerwester and colleagues, 1990) was the first widely used attempt to fix this. It factorised the term-document matrix so that words occurring in similar contexts land near each other. The idea matured into learned word vectors (word2vec, Mikolov and colleagues, 2013) and then into contextual sentence encoders.

The shared principle is the distributional hypothesis: a word is characterised by the company it keeps. An embedding of a chunk is a point in a space where distance approximates similarity of meaning.

The weaknesses are as old as the idea. Rare tokens such as identifiers have no company to keep, so they are poorly represented. And the geometry says nothing about whether two passages state the same fact or merely share a topic.
47f9b93a26:
Searching a million vectors exactly means a million dot products per query. Approximate nearest-neighbour methods trade a little recall for orders of magnitude of speed. The graph method HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, preprint 2016, journal 2018) became the common choice. Libraries and databases adopted it: FAISS (2017) for research and batch use, then pgvector (2021) as a Postgres extension, along with the dedicated vector databases.

In 2020 two papers set the pattern that RAG follows. Dense passage retrieval (Karpukhin and colleagues) showed that a trained bi-encoder could beat BM25 on open-domain question answering. The original RAG paper (Lewis and colleagues, 2020) coupled a retriever to a generator, so the generator conditioned on retrieved passages.

The paper trained the two jointly. Production systems today almost never do. They bolt a frozen retriever onto a frozen model and spend their effort on everything in this chapter.
53d31bfc91:
Once chat models could follow instructions, the obvious application was answering questions from a company's own documents. Teams quickly found that the demo did not survive contact with real estates. The demo had twenty clean PDFs, a fixed 1,000-token splitter and a vector store. Real estates have scanned contracts, tables, duplicated versions, permissions, and documents that change daily.

Over the same period, context windows grew from thousands of tokens to hundreds of thousands. Prompt caching made it cheap to resend a large prefix. Together these reopened the question of whether small corpora needed retrieval at all.

In September 2024 Anthropic published contextual retrieval. Before indexing, you ask a model to write a short context that situates each chunk within its document, and you index the chunk with that context attached. Section 13 explains it and measures the free version of it on the companion corpus.
4b4bed7987:
The pipeline around the index is not new either. A RAG ingestion job is an extract-transform-load job whose destination happens to be a search index. Change data capture, idempotent upserts, reconciliation against the system of record, blue/green migration of a read model, row-level security: a Spring Batch or Kafka Connect engineer has built every one of these.

The new transforms are parsing with structure, chunking and enrichment. The new failure is a silent retrieval miss, which produces a fluent wrong answer instead of an error. Treat the pipeline with the discipline of a data product and most of the problems become familiar ones.
2071012100: When a RAG system gives a bad answer, the instinct is to change the prompt or the model. Before you do, decide which of three faults produced it. Each lives at a different stage and has a different fix. The model can only work with what the retriever hands it, so all of these faults act before generation starts.
0ca0a0b937:
Fault A, the miss. The passage that contains the answer is not among the chunks returned. There are several reasons this happens:

  • it was never ingested (the parser dropped it, or the connector skipped the folder);
  • it was cut so that no single chunk holds the answer;
  • the embedding does not place it near the query;
  • a lexical match failed because the query used a synonym.

The model then answers from the neighbouring chunks, or from its own training data, with great fluency.
665fbcac5d:
Fault B, lost meaning. The right chunk was retrieved, but it cannot be interpreted, or it cannot be told apart from its twins. "The fee is waived in this case" does not say which fee or which case.

Here is the twin problem. Twenty customer contracts share the clause "If Customer terminates before month 24, Customer pays an early termination fee equal to 35 percent of the remaining Monthly Charges". A question about one named customer cannot be answered by text that does not contain the name. The retriever returns a plausible clause from the wrong agreement, and the model quotes it correctly.

Contextual retrieval was invented for this fault.
dbeed0c682: Fault C, the wrong audience. The chunk is relevant and correct, but the caller is not allowed to see it. By the time anyone notices, the content is already in the prompt. A prompt that says "do not reveal restricted material" cannot repair that. The fix has to be in the retrieval query, which means the index has to carry the data to filter on.
dc6ac42801:
Fault D, staleness, is a variant of A and C that deserves its own name. The index contains a version that the source no longer contains. The superseded price list is cited. The revoked permission still opens the document. The deleted contract still answers questions.

Staleness is an update-process fault, not a content fault. And it has an unusual property: it is invisible to any evaluation that runs on a frozen test set.
0108c13ebd:
The practical consequence is a diagnostic habit. For every bad answer in a review, open the retrieved chunks first and ask three questions in order:

  1. Was the answer text among them (fault A)?
  2. If it was, could a reader tell from the chunk alone which document, section and entity it came from (fault B)?
  3. Was this person allowed to see every chunk in the prompt, and was every chunk current (faults C and D)?

Only when the answers are yes, yes and yes do the model or the prompt become the suspect.

Companion example 07 gives a first sense of how much fault B matters. The corpus is 20 near-identical contracts, and the queries name a customer. A structure-aware pipeline with no context at all reaches a recall@5 of 0.37. The same pipeline with a title and section path in front of each chunk reaches 0.95. The model, the embedding and the query were identical in both runs.
a1e5bc18f7:
RAG solves one problem: the knowledge the model needs is larger than what you can, or want to, put in every request. You split the corpus into pieces, index them, and send only the pieces that look relevant. The price is a pipeline to build and run, plus a new failure mode, the retrieval miss.

The alternative is to put the whole corpus in the prompt and use prompt caching, so repeated requests do not pay full price for the shared prefix. Anthropic's contextual retrieval write-up gives a rule of thumb. If the knowledge base is smaller than about 200,000 tokens (roughly 500 pages), include it in the prompt, cache it, and skip retrieval.

An architect's job is to test that rule against the actual numbers. The rule hides three variables: how often the cache is warm, what the premium costs, and what the premium buys.
cd6e6418f0:
Use symbols so the comparison survives price changes. Let P be the base input price per token, C the corpus size in tokens, Q the instruction and question tokens, and ks the retrieved tokens (k chunks of s tokens each).

At the time of writing, prompt caching bills a cache write at about 1.25 times the base input price for the five-minute lifetime. A cache read costs about 0.1 times the base price. (Check the docs for current multipliers, the longer-lifetime option and its price, and the minimum cacheable length, which depends on the model.)

A cache entry lives for a fixed time after its last use, and each hit refreshes it. So whether a request pays the read price or the write price depends on whether another request arrived within the lifetime T. For roughly random arrivals at a rate of lambda per minute, the probability of a warm cache is 1 - exp(-lambda T). The expected input cost per request is then:
5bd5003671: A telecom device-support knowledge base is 150,000 tokens. A request carries 1,500 tokens of instructions and question. RAG would retrieve 8 chunks of 500 tokens, which is 4,000 tokens. Use an illustrative base price of 3 dollars per million input tokens, and substitute the current price for your model. Companion example 13 computes the table:
3a55938148:
Read the table the way you would read a capacity plan.

At one request per hour the cache is cold 92 percent of the time. Every cold request pays a 1.25 times write on 150,000 tokens. So cached long context costs more than not caching at all ($0.5256 against $0.4545).

At 60 requests per hour the cache is warm 99 percent of the time, and the request costs $0.053. Even fully warm it settles at $0.0495, against $0.0165 for RAG. Reading 150,000 tokens at one tenth of the price is still more tokens than reading 4,000 at full price. So at this corpus size, cached long context never beats RAG on input cost. It only gets close.

The premium is $0.033 per request, about $950 a day at 28,800 requests a day. The real question is not "which is cheaper". It is "is the premium worth what it buys?"
3a033d4f33:
What it buys is the absence of three things: retrieval misses, an index to operate, and chunking decisions. That turns the break-even into a statement about the cost of a miss. If RAG misses 5 percent of questions and each miss costs $0.66 in rework or escalation, the premium is paid back. If RAG misses 2 percent, a miss must cost more than $1.65.

This framing keeps you honest in both directions. Take a benefits handbook of 90,000 tokens. RAG misses 8 percent of questions there, because answers spread across sections, and a miss sends an employee to HR at an internal cost of $5. That favours long context with a cache: the premium is $0.04 a request against an expected miss cost of $0.40.

Now take an 80,000-token FAQ at 100 requests an hour, with 2 percent misses at $0.50 each. That favours RAG by a whisker ($0.012 against $0.010).

Those numbers are placeholders, so change them. The method is what the exam rewards.
4a031be051: CCAR-P rewards the simplest design that meets the stated numbers. If the corpus is 80,000 tokens, changes twice a year and is visible to everyone, a vector database is over-engineering. If the stem mentions per-customer data, access groups, or millions of documents, retrieval is required, and the question becomes how to build it well. Check the stem for the three hard constraints (size, visibility, change rate) before you look at anything else.
82b9616bdd: Chapter 1 introduced the requirements card: a one-page statement of the numbers a design must meet. A RAG system needs a few more rows than a plain model call, and every one of them decides something in the pipeline. Without these rows, a team tunes chunk sizes by intuition and argues about vector databases. With them, most design decisions become arithmetic.
67eacc2ed6:
The point about per-segment requirements being literal applies here exactly as it does elsewhere. Take an illustrative scenario that demands 95 percent accuracy for each contract type and 96 percent overall. You measure by type, and you fix any type below 95 percent before launch. An overall number that clears 96 while one type sits at 91 is a failed gate.

In a RAG system the segments are usually document types, products, regions or languages. Those are what differ in structure, and therefore in chunking. A single recall figure hides a table-heavy segment whose rows were flattened by the parser.
003097727d:
Turn the corpus row into chunk counts, vector storage and ingest cost. Take the runbooks. 9 million tokens at a target of about 400 tokens per chunk is 22,500 chunks. With a 1,024-dimension embedding stored as 32-bit floats, a vector is 4,096 bytes, so the vectors take about 92 MB.

An HNSW graph adds overhead that depends on its connectivity parameter, commonly tens of percent of the vector size (check the docs for your database). The text, metadata and lexical index add more. The whole thing still fits comfortably in the memory of one modest Postgres instance. That settles the choice of store before any vendor comparison.

Now the costs. Embedding 9 million tokens, plus about 15 percent more for prefixes, at an illustrative 0.12 dollars per million tokens costs around $1.24 for the backfill. Contextual retrieval over the same 9 million tokens (runbook pages of about 1,450 tokens cut into 3 or 4 chunks) comes to roughly 30 dollars at the illustrative small-model prices of companion example 08.

Neither number drives the decision. The drivers are the freshness SLO, the revocation SLO and the ACL model, and those cost engineering time rather than money.
c6c31e7a94:
Now scale the same arithmetic to a contract estate: 40,000 contracts averaging 18,000 tokens each. That is 720 million tokens and, at 350 tokens per chunk, about 2.06 million chunks. The vectors take about 8.4 GB before graph overhead. That is still a single large Postgres node, but it is no longer a laptop demo. The HNSW build takes hours, memory planning matters, and a filter that selects one customer out of 40,000 is the selective-filter case of section 19.

Contextual retrieval over 720 million tokens is a real line item. Each chunk call reads the whole document from the cache, so cost per document token grows with the number of chunks per document. At the illustrative prices of example 08, 18,000-token documents cut into 350-token chunks cost about 8.80 dollars per million document tokens. That is roughly $6,300 for the estate. Compare 3.84 dollars per million for the 8,000-token, 800-token-chunk shape in Anthropic's published estimate. It is worth testing on a sample before committing (section 14).

The same method gives different answers at different scale. The card is what tells you which scale you are at.
d7d3e10a1d:
An ingestion pipeline is a batch or streaming ETL job whose output is a search index. If you have built a Spring Batch job that reads from a source system, transforms records and writes to a store with idempotent upserts, you already know its shape. It has a reader, a chain of processors, a writer, a restart story, and a way to know that the destination matches the source.

The new parts are the transforms:

  • Parsing turns binary documents into text without losing structure.
  • Chunking decides the unit of retrieval.
  • Enrichment attaches metadata, access control and context.
  • Embedding turns text into vectors.

Each stage has its own failure mode, and the pipeline needs a change feed to stay correct.
c64349364a:
Four design properties apply to the pipeline as a whole. They recur through the rest of the chapter.

  1. idempotence: ingesting the same document twice must leave the index unchanged and cost nothing in embeddings. Change feeds deliver events at least once, and the worker will be restarted. A non-idempotent writer produces duplicates sooner or later.
  2. document-level atomicity: a reader must never see half of the old version and half of the new one. So the document is the unit of the transaction, and its chunks are children of it.
  3. determinism: the same input must produce the same chunks and the same chunk ids. Otherwise change detection degenerates into re-embedding everything. This is the argument for deterministic chunkers and stored contexts.
  4. observability: every stage emits counts (documents in, elements out, chunks out, chunks embedded, chunks rejected). A silent parser regression looks exactly like a normal day until a user complains.
c46edf9b6c:
Batch or streaming? Match the freshness SLO. A nightly crawl is fine for a handbook updated twice a year. It is wrong for a runbook estate with a 10-minute freshness target.

Most enterprise systems end up with both. An event-driven path gives speed: a webhook or a change feed from the source system into a queue, and a worker that re-ingests one document at a time. A scheduled full reconciliation compares the index with the source of truth and repairs drift. Sections 20 and 21 build both and measure what each one catches.
b5a86795c0:
Parsing turns PDF, DOCX, HTML, wiki pages or email into text. The common mistake is to extract a flat string and call it done.

Everything later in the pipeline depends on knowing where the headings, list items, table rows and page boundaries were. Structure is the only information about where one idea ends and the next begins. So a parser should emit a sequence of typed elements (heading with its level, paragraph, list item, table row with its header), each carrying its page number.

Each piece then feeds a later stage. From the headings the chunker derives the section path. From the table header it can restate each row in words. From the page number the citation can point a person to the right place in the source.
40206c4b89:
The small parser in the companion folder does four things worth copying:

  • It splits the document into pages on explicit markers.
  • It drops lines that repeat on at least 60 percent of pages after normalising digits. That removes headers, footers and "Page 3 of 9" without a list of patterns.
  • It maps a leading run of hash marks to a heading level (a stand-in for whatever heading information your real extractor provides).
  • It turns a pipe-delimited table into rows that remember their header.
4f21cabe6d:
Claude is itself a usable parser for hard documents. The Messages API accepts PDFs and images as input (check the docs for the current file size and page limits, and for how pages are tokenised). So you can send a scanned page and ask for Markdown with headings and tables preserved. This often beats a rule-based extractor on difficult layouts. But it costs tokens per page, and the arithmetic matters at scale.

Suppose a page costs roughly 2,000 input tokens when sent as a document (illustrative; the real figure depends on the content and the format, so check the docs). The contract estate is 40,000 contracts of 40 pages, and 8 percent of pages are scans. That is 128,000 scanned pages and about 256 million tokens. At the illustrative 3 dollars per million input tokens, that is about $770, plus the output. Sending all 1.6 million pages would cost more than twelve times that, and for native PDFs a cheaper extractor already works.

So route. Use the cheap extractor by default, detect pages with little or no text, and send only those to the model. Sample 100 pages from each route and measure the error rate before switching a route over.
b7d1b66bfd:
Broken: text = pdf_extract(path) followed by a 1,000-token splitter. The running header lands in the middle of clause 12.2. Every chunk contains "CONFIDENTIAL", so BM25 learns that "confidential" is a meaningless term. And no chunk knows its page.

Fixed: parse to typed elements, drop repeated lines by frequency, keep heading level and page, and make the chunker consume elements instead of text. The fix is about 60 lines (the code above), and it has no model call. Check it with one assertion that no element contains a known header string.
9f3be33b4e: A chunk is the unit of retrieval. The model usually sees a chunk alone, without its neighbours, so the chunk must answer two questions by itself. The retriever needs to know is this relevant to the query. The model needs to know what does this say, and about what. These pull in opposite directions, and the size of a chunk is a compromise between them.
c9ba6a58fc:
Consider the retriever first. An embedding summarises the whole chunk as one point in space. A chunk that mixes several ideas has an embedding that sits between them. A query about only one of those ideas scores lower against it than against a chunk about that idea alone.

A toy model shows the shape of the effect. Say a chunk contains m equally weighted, mutually unrelated ideas, and the query matches one of them exactly. The cosine similarity is about 1/sqrt(m): 1.0 for one idea, 0.5 for four, 0.33 for nine. Real encoders are less brutal and not linear, but the direction is right. It is why a 2,000-token chunk holding six clauses is a worse retrieval target for any one clause than six chunks.

Lexical scoring has the matching property. BM25 normalises by length, so a long chunk with one matching sentence scores below a short chunk with the same sentence.
ebb506df21:
Now the model. A short chunk often lacks the context that makes it meaningful: "The fee is waived in this case." Which fee, which case, in which agreement? Small chunks give sharp retrieval and thin meaning. Large chunks give rich meaning and blurred retrieval, and they also spend the prompt budget.

Here is the budget arithmetic. If the ceiling for an answer is $0.03 at 3 dollars per million input tokens, you can afford 10,000 input tokens in total. Subtract 1,500 for instructions and the question, and 8,500 remain. With k = 10 retrieved chunks, each can average at most 850 tokens. With k = 5, at most 1,700.

In practice the budget is rarely the binding constraint. The usual one is that tokens spent on irrelevant parts of large chunks push out other relevant chunks. The companion mini-lab (example 14) measures this directly. The top five chunks from a fixed 120-token chunker put 565 tokens into the prompt. The top five clause chunks put 129, for the same recall.
8a6fcd3036: There is no magic number that escapes the compromise. The way out is to cut along the boundaries the author already put in the document, so that each chunk is one idea by construction. Then you restore lost context explicitly with the section path, metadata and, where it pays, a model-written context. That gives four strategies, in order of increasing sophistication.
b5fb2ed9f9:
The code below implements all four, plus the chunk record. To stay dependency-free, it counts tokens approximately (four characters per token). In production, use the token counting endpoint, or a tokenizer close enough for budgeting (check the docs).

The structure-aware chunker takes typed elements from the parser. It has two modes, for two kinds of documents. In clause mode, a numbered paragraph starts a new chunk. In procedure mode, a whole section stays together as long as it fits, because a runbook step out of order is dangerous. Tables turn into one chunk per row, with the header restated as "Column: value".
899880eb20:
Two details in that code matter more than the algorithms.

First, every chunk carries a section_path. It later becomes metadata, and it also gets prepended to the text before embedding.

Second, a chunk has two possible ids. The ordinal id (doc#7) shifts when anything is inserted before the chunk. The section-keyed id (doc#12-termination#12.2) survives an insertion elsewhere. Section 12 and companion example 11 show what that difference costs.

Now run the four chunkers over the same 20 contracts and measure properties that do not need a model.
861fff29cf:
Read the columns as four separate defects.

clause_whole counts the 60 clauses we care about (fee, cap, breach notice in 20 contracts) that sit entirely inside at least one chunk. A clause that is cut cannot be cited cleanly. Fixed windows with no overlap leave 46 of 60 whole, so 14 clauses are cut. With 18 tokens of overlap, 50 of 60 stay whole. Recursive splitting keeps all 60 whole in this corpus, because clauses are separate lines and the recursive splitter prefers line breaks.

mixed counts chunks that contain clauses from more than one numbered section. Fixed chunks mix sections in 73 of 94 cases, recursive chunks in 55 of 100, and structure-aware chunks in none. A mixed chunk puts a fee beside a liability cap, where the model can quote one and cite the other.

density is the share of the chunk that is the answer for the fee clause. It is 0.27 to 0.29 for the window and recursive chunkers and 1.00 for the clause chunker. In other words, three quarters of what the first two put in the prompt is not the answer.

has_path shows that only the structure-aware chunker knows which section a chunk belongs to. A citation and a prefix both need that.
fa435b01a7:
A fair reading also records what the structure-aware chunker costs. It produced 321 chunks of 28 tokens on average, against 94 to 101 chunks of about 100 for the others. Small chunks mean more vectors, more rows, and a lexical index with fewer words per document.

The contracts in this synthetic corpus have very short clauses (about 25 tokens each). Real clauses run from 60 to 400 tokens, and the structure-aware chunker's average rises accordingly. The pipeline also has a minimum size (min_tok). Below it, a chunk merges into its predecessor in the same section, so a one-line definition does not become a chunk of its own. Treat both bounds as parameters to measure on your corpus.
e2b0303de9:
Semantic chunking embeds each sentence, computes the similarity of each adjacent pair, and cuts where similarity falls into the lowest percentile. It adapts to documents with no markup, such as call transcripts. That is its real use.

It has three costs that a scenario can turn into a trap:

  • It embeds every sentence at ingest, which is several times the cost of embedding the chunks.
  • Its boundaries depend on the embedding model and on neighbouring sentences. An edit anywhere in a paragraph can move boundaries downstream and make unchanged text look changed. That defeats hash-based change detection.
  • When retrieval is poor, there is no structural reason for a boundary to inspect. You can only tune a percentile.

If a document has headings, clauses or steps, use them. Reserve semantic chunking for sources that have nothing else.
ac4084bc9a:
Broken: 40,000 contracts, fixed 1,000-token windows, no section path. Clause 12.2 sits in two chunks, and the second also holds clause 13.1. Asked about the termination fee, the system returns the second chunk first (it mentions fees and caps), and the model cites the liability clause.

Fixed: parse numbered clauses and chunk one clause per unit with a section path. Prepend title and path to the indexed text. Keep overlap near zero, because clause boundaries are clean. Then re-measure recall on a labelled set by contract type. Do not touch the model, k, or the overlap first. None of them addresses a clause being cut.
a6f1e6228e: No chunking strategy is best in general. The strategy follows the structure of the source and the shape of the questions asked of it. The table maps the corpora that appear in telecom, retail and policy work to their natural unit and a starting size. The sizes are starting points for the experiment in section 31, and every one is a hypothesis until measured.
175e3b1371: Tables deserve a worked example, because they are where flat extraction does the most visible harm. A rate-plan table extracted as cell text reads "Plus 50GB / 50GB / $65/mo / 15GB / Canada and Mexico". A question about hotspot data for the Unlimited Plus plan retrieves a row. But no chunk says which number is the hotspot allowance. One chunk per row, written with its column names, answers it directly:
6b5cb935ab:
The same example handles a ticket thread. In the raw thread, the customer's first message appears three times: once as the original and twice as quoted history in later replies. Left alone, it becomes three near-identical chunks. They crowd the top-k and teach the lexical index that the message is three times as important. After cleaning, each message is a chunk with the thread id as metadata.

Some questions are really calculations over a table ("which plan is cheapest per gigabyte?"). For those, neither chunking nor retrieval is the right tool. The better design is a SQL tool in front of a structured copy of the table, which chapter 9 covers.
e18f391b24:
One more technique resolves the size compromise at query time. Index small chunks for sharp matching. When one matches, send its parent (the whole section, or the chunk plus its neighbours) to the model. You get the precision of small embeddings and the context of large passages.

It costs more prompt tokens per hit, so you usually lower k. It also requires the chunk record to know its parent. The section-keyed id gives you that for free: the parent of doc#12-termination#12.2 is every chunk whose id starts doc#12-termination#.

Use it when answers depend on neighbouring clauses, such as a definition, or an exception that follows the rule. Then verify with the labelled set that the longer context improves the answer rather than diluting it.
120dccb350:
Overlap repeats the last few sentences of chunk N at the start of chunk N+1. It protects against facts that straddle a boundary. That matters when boundaries are arbitrary, as in fixed-size and sometimes recursive chunking.

The cost has three parts:

  • Index size grows by a factor s / (s - o) for chunk size s and overlap o. So 20 percent overlap means 25 percent more chunks to embed, store and search.
  • The same passage can come back twice in the top-k, spending slots on duplicates.
  • Overlap hides the underlying problem, a boundary in the wrong place, instead of fixing it.
04e935a48e: Fixed or recursive chunking: 10 to 20 percent overlap is a reasonable default. The one thing it reliably buys is fewer cut facts. Measure whether that matters on your corpus before paying for it.
b475b098ce: A chunk in the index is not just text. It is a record. The fields on that record decide which questions the system can answer correctly, which ones it can answer only for the right people, and how cheaply it can be updated. Decide the fields from the requirements card before you build the pipeline. Adding a field later means re-ingesting everything.
520e75cab5:
Suppose the id is doc#ordinal. Inserting one paragraph near the start of a document shifts every later ordinal. A change detector compares id by id, so it sees different text under the same id for every chunk after the insertion, and re-embeds every one. Worse, every stored citation that named doc#12 now points at a different clause.

A section-keyed id (doc#12-termination#12.2, built from the last heading and the clause label) survives an edit elsewhere in the document. It depends only on where the chunk sits in the structure.

Which scheme is right depends on how the source changes. Append-only logs suit ordinals. Edited contracts suit section keys. Companion example 11 measures the difference on one contract with five kinds of change:
d6d501a09c:
The content hash is computed over the indexed text (context, path and body), not just the body. That is deliberate. If the title changes, the prefix changes, and the vector must be recomputed.

The ACL is deliberately left out of the hash. A permission change must reach the index within the revocation SLO, and it must get there without paying for an embedding call. That is the "ACL change only" row above: zero embedded, every chunk updated in place.
3ccae7a298:
Contextual retrieval attacks fault B directly. Before a chunk is embedded and indexed, a model writes a short context (50 to 100 tokens) that situates the chunk within its document. That context is prepended to the chunk, and the contextualised text is what both the embedding and the lexical index see.

Anthropic's example makes the point. The raw chunk "The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter" matches almost nothing specific. Now add context: "This chunk is from an SEC filing on ACME corp's performance in Q2 2023; the previous quarter's revenue was $314 million. The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter." That version matches a query about ACME's Q2 2023 revenue growth, both semantically and lexically.
305509e680:
Anthropic reported three results on its test sets. Contextual embeddings reduced the top-20 retrieval failure rate by 35 percent (from 5.7 to 3.7 percent). Contextual embeddings combined with contextual BM25 reduced it by 49 percent (to 2.9 percent). Adding a reranker reduced it by 67 percent (to 1.9 percent).

Treat these as evidence that the technique helps, and as a prompt to measure. Your corpus will not reproduce the same numbers. Chapter 11 covers how to measure it, and chapter 9 covers reranking.
88b0b05190:
In a structured corpus, much of the missing context is already in your parser output: the document title and the section path. Prepending them costs nothing and is deterministic.

On the companion corpus of 20 near-identical contracts, the experiment has four arms:

  • chunk text alone;
  • document title in front;
  • title and section path in front;
  • a model-written context.

The retrieval, the embedder and the 78 labelled questions are identical across arms.
bc53aed674:
Read the result honestly.

The jump from 0.37 to 0.88 is the whole story of fault B. The name of the customer was missing from 19 of every 20 relevant chunks, and putting the title in front fixed it for no money. The step from 0.88 to 0.95 is the section path.

The last step, the model-written context, shows 1.00 in this table. But in this run the model is a scripted stand-in. It builds its sentence from the very same title and heading, so it carries no more information than the free prefix. The small gain comes from repeating the customer's name in the text, which gives it more weight. Do not read that row as evidence about a real model on real contracts.

What the experiment does establish is the order of operations. Measure the free prefix first, because on a corpus with clean structure it captures most of the gain. Spend model calls only where a labelled set shows a gap that the free prefix leaves.
be6b250026: Corpora with weak or no structure: emails, chat logs, call transcripts, scraped pages. There is no section path to prepend. A model-written sentence ("This message is from the thread about the Q3 outage in the Dallas data centre, replying to the proposal to fail over...") is the only way to add what the chunk omits.
fed3e6a083: Coreference and implicit subjects: chunks that say "the Company", "this Section", "the Fee", "it". The model can resolve them from the whole document. A title cannot.
7298086d6f: Cross-references: a clause that says "subject to clause 14.3" can carry a short note on what 14.3 says. This is also where hallucinated context does the most damage, so check a sample by eye.
e72d3e72f8:
Calling a model during ingestion brings three engineering problems that the deterministic prefix does not have.

The first is stability. In practice a model's output varies between runs, even at temperature zero. If the context is regenerated on every ingest, the index text changes every time. The content hash changes too, and every chunk is re-embedded on every run.

The fix is to store each generated context, keyed by the document id, the document version and the chunk text, and to call the model only on a miss. A re-ingest after one clause changes then calls the model once. The companion class does exactly that.
5a608e734f:
The second is staleness. The context was written when the document had a certain title, a certain set of parties and a certain version. If a later version renames the customer, every stored context for that document is wrong in the same way. Key the store by document version, so a new version invalidates its contexts. And decide explicitly whether an amendment to one clause should regenerate the contexts of the others. Usually it should not, unless the amended clause changes definitions.

The third is trust. The document text goes into a prompt, and documents are untrusted input. A hostile or careless document can contain text that looks like instructions. The context prompt asks for one short sentence, and the output goes into an index, not into a tool call, so the blast radius is small. Even so, limit the output's length and store it as data, never executed. Have a person read a sample of contexts before the backfill. Chapter 13 treats injection more generally.
2572992db5:
The document goes in the system block with cache_control, and the chunk goes in the user turn. The model is a small, fast tier (the companion uses claude-haiku-4-5; check the docs for current model ids and prices). This is an offline job, so latency does not matter. That is the reason to use the cheapest tier that writes acceptable contexts.

Chapter 5 explains the caching mechanics. The next section works out what this call pattern costs, and the three ways it quietly stops working.
a99be4b092: The cost of contextual retrieval is the cost of one model call per chunk, with the document as a shared prefix. If the prefix is cached, the first call pays a write. Each later call for that document pays the read price, plus the fresh chunk and instruction tokens and the output. Take a document of D tokens cut into n chunks of s tokens, with a prompt of q tokens, an output of o tokens and prices P (input) and P_out (output):
e71f9529a4:
Two consequences follow.

First, the reads are usually the dominant term. For fixed chunk size, (n-1) * 0.1 * D grows with the square of the document length. A longer document has more chunks, and each of them reads the whole document. That is why a 100-page contract costs far more per token than a 5-page one.

Second, the cost per million document tokens depends on the shape of the corpus. A published estimate is only valid for the shape it assumed. Anthropic estimated about 1.02 dollars per million document tokens for 8,000-token documents, 800-token chunks, 50 tokens of instructions and 100 tokens of context. The companion reproduces that to within about six percent using small-model prices of 0.25 and 1.25 dollars per million tokens. It then recomputes it for other shapes at the illustrative prices of 1.00 and 5.00 used here:
1218f590c1: The same shape-dependence shows up in the choice of chunk size. Halving the chunk size roughly doubles the number of calls and the read cost. So a finer chunking pays for itself only if it improves recall. Run the experiment on a sample (a few hundred documents) and extrapolate with the formula before committing a backfill.
0eb899f079:
The saving depends on the cache behaving. When it doesn't, it fails quietly: nothing errors, and the bill is simply larger.

Companion example 08 uses a scripted client whose cache semantics are modelled on the real ones. A prefix is readable only after the call that wrote it has finished. A prefix below a minimum length is not cached, and the minimum is model-specific, so check the docs. The example runs the same 24 chunks four ways.
74ee1652fb: Fan-out before the first response (case B). The cache entry becomes readable only after the first call has produced a response. If you submit all of a document's chunk calls concurrently, they all miss, and each pays the 1.25 times write on the whole document. That is worse than not caching. Make the first call for each document, wait for it, then fan out the rest. Parallelism across documents is fine. Parallelism within a document is the trap.
8529f8262a: A prefix below the minimum length (case C). Prompt caching has a minimum cacheable length that depends on the model (check the docs for the current figures; they are in the low thousands of tokens). A shorter prefix is processed normally without any error, and both cache counters in the usage object stay at zero. For short documents this does not matter. But it explains why a cost estimate built on cache reads comes out too low when the corpus is made of one-page pages.
f7e3d117e0: No cache marker, or a prefix that changes (case D). Every call is a miss if the cache control marker is missing, or if anything before it differs between calls (a timestamp in the system prompt, a request id, an instruction block that varies). The check is the usage object. In a healthy run, cache_read_input_tokens is much larger than cache_creation_input_tokens. Put that ratio on the ingestion dashboard and alert on it.
8814da3c8c:
For large backfills, the Message Batches API offers a substantial discount for work that does not need an answer in seconds. A contextual-retrieval backfill is exactly that kind of work. Check the docs for how batching and caching combine, because the cache behaviour in batches is not guaranteed in the same way.

Two more levers deserve a line. If documents are short and numerous, caching may not apply, and plain batching is the saving. If the corpus is huge, run the experiment on a stratified sample and compare against the free prefix. Then extend the model-written context only to the document types where the gain justified the dollars.
1aa0e7c0e7:
An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector so that texts with similar meaning are close, usually under cosine similarity. Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model. Its documentation points to third-party providers such as Voyage AI (check the docs for the current recommendations and for the options available on your cloud).

So the decision is a dependency selection. The criteria are the ones you would use for any dependency, plus a few specific to retrieval.
f7348558e4:
The toy embedder in the companion folder shows what an embedding is, without hiding anything. It does four things:

  • It maps words through a small concept table, so "cancel", "terminate" and "exit" land on the same feature. This stands in for what a trained model learns.
  • It adds hashed word pairs.
  • It adds character bigrams and trigrams. That is why two identifiers one digit apart end up near each other, a property real models also show.
  • It normalises the vector to length one, so a dot product is a cosine.

It is deliberately weak, and that is what makes it useful: its failures are legible.
644b8e468c:
Three habits follow from treating the embedding model as a versioned dependency.

  • Record the model name on every row (the embed_model field), so that mixed-model vectors are detected rather than silently compared.
  • Assert at ingest that ntok(index_text) is below the model's input limit, and count truncations as a metric. A 4,000-token chunk quietly cut to 512 tokens loses most of its content without an error.
  • Embed queries with the same preprocessing as documents, minus the prefix. The query does not have a title.
35208d3419:
Dense vectors capture meaning. "What does it cost to leave the agreement early?" matches a clause about an "early termination fee" with no shared words.

They are weak on exact tokens: a part number SM-G998U, an alarm code ERR-5G-4471, a plan name. An embedding compresses a rare string into a point that looks like the points of other rare strings. So ERR-5G-4471 lands near ERR-5G-4417.

Lexical scoring is the opposite: excellent at exact rare terms and blind to synonyms. So build an index pair, one of each kind, from the same chunk text. The retriever can then use whichever one fits the query. Chapter 9 shows how to combine them with reciprocal rank fusion, and when to weight one over the other.
6540ff22cd: BM25, the lexical scoring function, is small enough to read in full. Take a query term t, a document d of length L, an average length avgL, a term frequency f, and the free parameters k1 (about 1.2 to 2) and b (about 0.75):
31183d6ab8: The first factor, idf, is large for a rare term and near zero for a common one. That is why a query containing an alarm code is dominated by the alarm code. The fraction saturates in f, so the tenth occurrence adds little. The length term makes a long chunk with one matching word score below a short chunk with the same word. b controls how much: 0 turns length normalisation off, and 1 applies it fully.
