bf7f537e0d:
Now measure the two failure modes on the companion corpus. The first experiment asks five paraphrase questions of a single contract. None of them shares a word with the answer clause ("what is the charge for premature exit"). The second queries twelve runbooks by their alarm code.

One caution about reading the numbers. The toy embedder's concept table was written by hand to behave like a trained model on exactly this vocabulary. So the paraphrase result shows the direction of the effect, not its size.
2854a1761d:
One last observation from the mini-lab belongs here, because it surprises people. On this corpus, most questions share words with their answers. Lexical search alone scored recall@5 of 1.00, the toy vector search 0.86, and a fusion of the two 0.95.

Fusion landed below the best single list. Rank fusion with equal weights pulled in weak vector results for one query kind: queries about payment terms, where the toy vectors failed completely. With real embeddings the balance changes, so measure it.

The lesson is general, though. Combining retrievers is a decision with a measurable effect, not an automatic improvement, and chapter 9 treats it as one.
c75d0e1b81:
For an enterprise team that already runs Postgres, pgvector plus built-in full-text search is often the simplest architecture that works. One store gives you:

  • transactional upserts;
  • row-level filtering with ordinary WHERE clauses;
  • joins to the tables that hold your ACLs;
  • backups and monitoring you already operate;
  • a team that knows how to tune it.

Dedicated vector databases and search engines also have their place. That includes OpenSearch and Elasticsearch, which have lexical scoring, vector search and filters in one engine, and the managed vector services. They make sense at larger scale, at higher query rates, when you need features Postgres lacks, or when the platform team already runs one.

Whichever you choose, the schema questions are the same. The sizing arithmetic of section 05 is the test of whether Postgres is enough. 22,500 chunks and 2 million chunks are both comfortable. 200 million is a different conversation.
249c0ff78e: A caution on the lexical side. Postgres ts_rank and ts_rank_cd are not BM25. They lack inverse-document-frequency saturation and BM25's length normalisation. They are good enough for many corpora, and bad at long documents with repeated terms. Extensions that add true BM25 scoring exist (check the docs for the current options). If exact-match behaviour is central, as in the alarm-code case, test the lexical side explicitly. Don't assume parity with a search engine.
aada61c65e:
Three features of that schema are deliberate.

The check constraint on acl_groups makes an unlabelled chunk impossible to store. A connector bug that drops permissions then fails loudly at ingest. Without it, the bug would quietly open the document to everyone. And if the application treats an empty list as "no restriction", nobody would notice.

Both query shapes put the tenant, currency and ACL tests in the WHERE clause, so the planner and the index can use them.

The row-level security policy is a second line of defence. It does not replace the application filter, since the application filter also carries group membership. But it means a missing or wrong tenant filter cannot return another tenant's rows.

The tuning knobs that matter:
6f44e9bc2e:
A retrieval system sits between a large body of documents with permissions and a model that will repeat whatever it is shown. The model cannot know who the user is or what they may see. It receives text. So the only place to enforce visibility is before the text reaches the prompt, which means in the retrieval query. And the query can enforce it only if the index stores what the filter needs.

That is why ACL metadata appears in the ingestion section of a chapter about chunking. It is a property of each chunk: captured at ingest, refreshed on change, and checked on every query. Chapter 7 covers how the caller's identity and group memberships are established and propagated. This section covers what the index must hold and how the query must use it.
edd55c323d:
Copy the permission information from the source system at ingest. Store it on each chunk as a list of group or principal identifiers that may read it, plus the tenant.

Keep the source system as the authority, and treat the copy as a cache with an SLO. When permissions change at the source, the change feed carries the event. The worker updates the ACL on the affected chunks without re-embedding anything, because the text did not change. A reconciliation job repairs any event that was lost.

Two design questions come up every time.
b79c0caf60:
Expand groups at ingest or at query? Suppose you expand nested groups when ingesting, so each chunk stores the flattened set of users. Then changing a group's membership changes thousands of chunks, and the revocation SLO becomes a mass-update problem.

Now suppose you store the group identifiers on the chunk and expand the user's memberships at query time (from the verified token or a directory lookup). The chunk ACLs then only change when the document's own permissions change. Group churn costs nothing in the index.

Prefer query-time expansion of the user, with a bounded list of groups in the filter. The trade-off is a longer filter value for users who belong to hundreds of groups. Measure it, and if needed, mitigate it by mapping to coarser access labels.
be8a7221cb: What does a missing ACL mean? It means deny. A chunk with no ACL, or an empty one, is invisible to everyone. A database constraint (section 17) can make an unlabelled chunk impossible to store. The other convention, where absence means public, turns a connector bug into a data breach. Companion example 09 checks the deny rule explicitly.
b494cbd829:
Post-filtering fails for two separate reasons. If it runs after generation, the model has already seen the forbidden text. If it runs after retrieval but before generation, it leaves too few results. The top ten by similarity were all restricted, the filter removes ten, and the user gets nothing. Worse, the model gets nothing and answers from its training data.

Companion example 09 demonstrates both failures. A NOC engineer without the core-network group asks about an AMF fault. The unfiltered top three are all from the restricted runbook. Post-filtering returns zero rows. The pre-filter returns three visible rows.

A related trap: the search function in a library is often written with an optional filter. The companion's search methods take the filter as a required argument, so omitting it is a type error instead of an open index. The only way to search without restrictions is to construct a deliberately named evaluation_only filter.
3fe181fab0:
Notice what the last example prints. With the pre-filter, the engineer in noc-all who asks about ERR-5G-4471 gets three runbooks that are visible but irrelevant to the question.

The index did its job. The system now has a different problem. When the best visible matches are poor, the answer should be "I could not find that in the documents you can access", not a confident paraphrase of an unrelated page.

That behaviour needs a score threshold or a minimum evidence rule. Those belong to retrieval strategy (chapter 9) and guardrails (chapter 13). It also needs testing with the same labelled approach, using questions whose answers the caller is not allowed to see.
71d5e79cf9:
One last subtlety: every path that reads chunks must go through the filter, not only the primary search. Three paths can each become a side door if they query by id alone:

  • small-to-big retrieval that fetches a parent section by id;
  • neighbour expansion that reads the previous and next chunk;
  • citation lookups that return source text.

Route all of them through the same authorised read, and include them in the leak test below.
1efb70003d:
Pick each identity you care about: an engineer, a core engineer, a user from another tenant, a user with no groups. For each one and each restricted document, issue queries that would retrieve it, using every search path (vector, lexical, hybrid, parent fetch). Assert that no returned chunk is outside the identity's visibility.

Companion example 09 runs 3 queries per runbook across three search modes and reports 0 leaks for four identities. Run it in CI against a copy of the real ACL model, and again after every change to the filter code. This is the test that turns "we think retrieval is safe" into a number.
08281795cf:
Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes find candidates by walking a graph. In some implementations the walk produces a fixed number of candidates before any filter is applied. In pgvector's HNSW index, as the author understands it (check the docs for your version), the index scan yields up to ef_search candidates ordered by similarity. The WHERE clause is then applied to those candidates.

So if a caller can see 2 percent of the table, about 2 percent of the candidates survive. A query that asked for 10 rows may return 0 to 3. No error is raised. The user sees a thin answer, and only the smallest customers see it. That makes it hard to notice in aggregate metrics, and an excellent source of an exam scenario about "results missing for small customers".
389ed69024: Companion example 10 simulates the effect. It uses 2,000 chunks, 40 of them (2 percent) belonging to the small tenant, a query for 10 rows, and five strategies.
46f1f02d43: Raise ef_search. Easy, but it has to scale linearly with how selective the filter is. A caller who owns 0.1 percent of the table would need ef_search in the thousands. That makes every query slow for the sake of the smallest tenants.
f62239732b: Iterative index scans. Newer versions of pgvector can keep scanning until enough rows pass the filter, up to a configured limit (check the docs for your version and the exact setting names). This fixes the shortfall, at the price of variable latency for selective filters. Cap the scan and monitor the tail.
9c6fd176f4: Partition or index per tenant. A large tenant gets its own partition or partial index, and the long tail stays in the shared one. You get predictable latency, but more objects to create, migrate and monitor.
3d0a34749e: Exact search over the filtered set. For a small tenant, a sequential scan of its rows is both exact and fast. The planner may choose it when the filter is selective enough. Know when your planner does so.
32fa42be85: Building the index once is a demo. Keeping it correct is the system. Five kinds of change arrive, and each needs different handling. The table doubles as the list of events your change feed must carry.
0b31b5f282:
The ingest function is where these rules live. Read the companion's version as a specification. It does the following:

  • parses and chunks;
  • computes the indexed text and its hash for each chunk;
  • embeds only the chunks whose hash is new or whose embedding model differs;
  • handles the ACL-only case by updating metadata in place;
  • stages the writes and applies them together;
  • deletes chunk ids that are no longer produced.
2b6e1e18ac:
Three properties of that function deserve to be stated as invariants, because each can be tested (section 26).

  • Idempotence: running ingest(doc) twice in a row leaves the index unchanged and embeds nothing the second time.
  • Locality: a change to one clause embeds one chunk (given section-keyed ids), not the document.
  • Monotonic correctness: after ingest, the set of chunk ids for the document equals the set the chunker produces for the current version. So a deleted clause cannot linger as an orphan that still answers questions.
cf6a6cb9f8:
Versions deserve a policy rather than a default. A contract amendment supersedes clause 12.2 but not the rest. A policy version supersedes the previous one in full from a date. And questions come in two kinds: "what is the rule now" and "what was the rule on the sale date".

Store effective_from and effective_to on every chunk. Filter on is_current for the first kind of question and on the date range for the second.

Then decide per corpus whether superseded chunks are kept or deleted. Keeping them costs storage and adds the risk of a wrong filter. Deleting them is simpler, but then "as of" questions cannot be answered. A retail policy assistant that must answer with the policy in force at the time of sale needs them kept.
29ca4cd7c6:
An SLO such as "95 percent of edits searchable within 10 minutes" is a statement about a queue, and the queue has parts. An event waits for the worker's next poll. That wait is uniform between zero and the polling interval, so half the interval on average. It then waits behind earlier events in the queue. Then it takes the processing time: parsing, embedding, writing.

With a 5-minute poll and about 25 seconds of work per edit, the lag of a lightly loaded system sits between 25 seconds and 5 minutes 25 seconds. The p95 is close to the top of that range, plus queueing during bursts.

So choosing the polling interval is arithmetic against the SLO. A 10-minute p95 with a 5-minute poll leaves about 5 minutes of slack for queueing and work. That is fine for 40 edits a day and not fine for 4,000. Where an event-driven trigger exists (a webhook that puts a message on a queue), the poll wait disappears, and the SLO is mostly processing time.
b7e8a55841:
Permission revocation is the same arithmetic with higher stakes. Between a revoke at the source and its effect in the index, a person who should no longer see a document still can. Call that interval the exposure window.

The exposure window is the lag of the ACL update path. That path should be a separate, fast lane. It needs no parsing or embedding, so it should process in seconds, with priority over content edits.

Companion example 12 simulates a working day on the twelve runbooks: 40 edits, a revocation, and three lost events (a deletion, an edit and a second revocation).
1e3bdb0944:
Change feeds lose events. They deliver them out of order. Or they never fire for a class of change nobody enabled: a permission change on a parent folder, a move between spaces, a restore from trash.

The simulation drops three events on purpose and prints the drift. There is one stale version, one orphaned set of chunks for a document that no longer exists at the source, and one mismatched ACL. Nothing in the pipeline noticed, because nothing had been sent.

The fix is the one you apply behind an event-driven billing system: a ledger reconciliation. Periodically compare the set of (document id, version, ACL hash) in the source with the set in the index. Repair differences by running the normal ingest. Two cadences cover different risks.
912a25cf02: ACL-only reconciliation every 15 minutes. Pull document ids and permission hashes from the source and from the index, and compare. It reads no content and writes only where ACLs differ, so it is cheap. It is what bounds the exposure window for lost revocations, at about the cadence plus the update time.
11230ef8f7: Full reconciliation nightly (or weekly for large estates). Compare ids, versions and etags. Find orphans (indexed but gone from the source), missing documents (at the source but not indexed) and stale versions, and repair them. It also catches parser regressions that changed chunk counts.
4181c1ad9b: State both cadences as requirements and monitor their results. The number of repairs per run is a health signal. A reconciliation that finds nothing for months is working. One that suddenly repairs hundreds of ACLs means the feed broke, and you want to know on the day it did.
2968869818:
Vectors from different embedding models are not comparable. Neither are chunks from different chunkers: ids, boundaries and the text each vector represents all change. So a model upgrade or a chunking change is a migration of a read model. Use the pattern you would use for a schema change on a service that cannot go down:

  1. Build the new index beside the old one from the same sources.
  2. Backfill it.
  3. Evaluate both on the same labelled queries.
  4. Switch reads by changing an alias or a configuration value.
  5. Keep the old index for a fixed period, so a rollback is one assignment, and then retire it.
29ea446540: Write the switching rule down before running the comparison. A rule written afterwards bends toward the result. A good rule has three parts: an overall gain threshold, a per-segment non-regression bound, and the governance tests. Companion example 15 migrates from a toy embedder without a concept table (A) to one with it (B).
d4ed279121:
The first candidate wins by 34 points of recall@5 overall, and it is still rejected. Queries about payment terms fell from 0.20 to 0.00, and the rule says no segment may drop by more than 2 points. The same guide-authored practice rule applies to this migration: an overall improvement does not pay for a regression in a segment you are obliged to serve.

The regression points at the cause. The new vocabulary table has no entry for "pay" and "invoice". The second candidate fixes that, and the rule then passes with a 42-point gain and no segment lower.

After the switch, a live monitor that reads a drop in recall on production traffic triggers the rollback in a single assignment. That is possible only because the old index and the alias were kept. The mixing guard in the example refuses to write a row embedded with one model into an index built with another. It turns a silent quality drop into an error.
2531e93994: The same pattern applies when the chunker changes, with two additions. First, chunk ids change, so stored citations from earlier answers no longer resolve. If citations are persisted (in tickets, in audit logs), keep a mapping from old ids to new, or keep the old index readable for audit. Second, re-run the leak test on the candidate before the switch. A new chunker is a new place for an ACL to go missing.
6cece2a984:
With the pieces in place, the path from a question to an answer is short. The identity comes from the authenticated session. The retriever turns it into a filter, runs the vector and lexical searches under that filter, fuses them, and fills the prompt up to a token budget. The prompt wraps each chunk with its id and path so the model can cite it.

After the model answers, a cheap check confirms that every cited id was among the chunks the caller was allowed to receive. The check does not prove the answer is right. It proves the citations are real. That catches a class of fabrication at almost no cost, and gives the user something to click.
b04c79bf32:
The example runs two scripted models. One cites a chunk it was given. The other cites a chunk id it never saw. The check passes the first and rejects the second. When the check fails, the safe action is to withhold the answer. Return "could not verify" and log the trace, so the failure is visible in the monitoring of chapter 10.

The last lines show the authorisation rule end to end. Asked as a user without the core-network group, the same question about ERR-5G-4471 retrieves four visible but irrelevant runbooks. Asked as a core engineer, it retrieves the right one.

Anthropic's API also offers a citations feature and a search-result content block designed for this pattern. They let the model return structured citations pointing into the supplied sources (check the docs for the current availability and block formats). Either way, the principle is the same: constrain citations to supplied ids.
821a9a2041:
The Python above is the specification. In a Spring codebase the same pipeline maps onto familiar parts. The point of showing it is that nothing here is foreign to a Java architect.

The reader is a Spring Batch ItemReader over the change feed. The processors are parse, chunk and enrich. The writer is a transactional upsert. Spring AI supplies abstractions for the ETL shape (document readers, transformers such as a token text splitter, and a VectorStore that embeds on write), for chat clients and for filter expressions.

What it does not decide for you is everything this chapter spent its length on: structure-aware chunking, stable ids, ACL semantics, change detection, reconciliation.
87386bdb4c:
First, the plain Java version in the companion. It compiles and runs with only the JDK (java PlainJavaPipeline.java). It implements:

  • structure-aware chunking on numbered clauses;
  • a section-keyed id and a SHA-256 content hash;
  • the idempotent document-level upsert with an embedding counter;
  • ACL-only updates and deletion of vanished chunks;
  • BM25 under an ACL pre-filter.
e7c19a4de7:
In a Spring service, the upsert is a method on a bean whose transaction boundary is the document. That mirrors how you would treat an aggregate in a domain-driven design: the document is the aggregate root, and its chunks are its children.

Here is the same operation on Spring AI abstractions. It compiles only with Spring Boot and Spring AI on the classpath. The class and method names follow Spring AI 1.x as the author knows it, and they have moved between milestones and releases. So check the docs for your version before copying it: document accessors, the search request builder, filter operators, upsert semantics of the store.
46879a5c54:
Two choices in that code are deliberate.

The ACL-only update bypasses the VectorStore abstraction and uses SQL against the underlying table. An abstraction whose write path embeds text is the wrong tool for a metadata change that must not embed anything.

The search builds its filter from the verified identity passed in by the caller, never from a parameter the model can set. You may use the Spring AI advisor mechanism for retrieval-augmented chat (the framework ships question-answering advisors, check the docs). If so, apply the same rules to whatever filter it receives: put the identity-derived expression in the request, not in a prompt.
2af26f48db:
For the ingestion job itself, a chunk-oriented Spring Batch step maps onto the pipeline directly. A reader pulls changed document ids from the queue. A processor returns the list of chunks, or null to skip an unchanged document. A writer calls the transactional upsert.

Make the step restartable by keying on document id and version. Put a skip policy on parse failures so that one corrupt PDF does not stall the queue. Route skipped documents to a dead-letter table and count them, since a rising count is the first sign of a parser regression (section 25).
a394fe6c70: An index that nobody monitors drifts. The metrics below are cheap to compute from the index and the pipeline's own counters, and each one detects a specific fault. Chapter 10 covers the observability platform around them, including traces of retrieved chunk ids per answer. This section lists the signals that belong to the index itself.
56656fc9cd:
The parser regression is the instructive one. Six contracts arrived as a single long line, so the chunker saw one paragraph per document. The median chunks per document fell from 15 to 3. Nothing errored, and ingest counts looked normal. Retrieval over those six contracts would have degraded to coarse paragraphs without any exception. A monitor on chunks per document catches it on the first run.

The same discipline applies to quality. Sample 50 retrieved sets a week for human review, track recall on the labelled set on a schedule, and add every production failure to the set (chapter 11).
4180099aec: Almost every property in this chapter can be tested with no model and no network. The pipeline is deterministic code with a fake embedder and a scripted client. Those tests run on every commit. The labelled evaluation runs on a schedule, because it is slower and statistical, and chapter 11 covers it. Here is the list of what to test. Companion example 18 implements 15 of them with unittest.
9a7ebb0d80: In a Spring project the equivalent is a JUnit suite with two pieces. A stub EmbeddingModel stands in for the real one and counts calls. Testcontainers runs real Postgres with pgvector for the SQL filters. You need the real database because the semantics of acl_groups && :groups, and of the planner under a selective filter, are properties of the database that a mock cannot show.
a002d38c3e:
Domain 5 asks that safety and compliance be built into the design rather than added at the end. A RAG pipeline has an unusually large governance surface. It copies an organisation's documents, derives new data from them (chunks, embeddings, generated contexts), sends them to third-party services, and feeds the results to a model.

Chapter 14 covers the regulatory frameworks (GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP and SOX or CPNI examples) in depth. The design decisions this chapter owns are these.
1c40ef3cd8:
Two of these are easy to underestimate.

First, embeddings are derived data. A vector can leak information about the text it came from. A deletion request that removes the document but leaves its vectors, its stored contexts and its cached prefixes has not removed the data. Design the deletion path to touch every derived store, and test it by deleting a document and searching for it.

Second, the index is a second copy of the estate. Whoever can read the vector store can read the content of every document in it. So the access model of the index store belongs in the same review as the access model of the source systems.

Whether a particular deployment satisfies a particular regulation is a question for your compliance function. The architect's job is to make the controls possible and the evidence cheap.
1f6cfdc983: CCAR-P presents scenarios with four plausible options and asks for the best architectural judgement. For RAG the pattern is consistent. The right answer changes the data design: whether to retrieve, the unit of chunking, the metadata, where the filter runs, how updates propagate. The wrong answers add model capacity or prompt text. Work each scenario before reading the reasoning.
45cdcfcce8:
The corpus is small, static and visible to everyone, so all three hard constraints point to long context. At 30 requests an hour the cache is warm 99 percent of the time (section 4), and the premium over RAG is about $0.04 per request. The reported failure (answers spread across sections) is exactly the case where retrieval hides information the model needs together.

Options 1, 2 and 4 improve a retrieval system that should not exist for this corpus. What matters is the expected-value comparison, not a rule. If RAG missed 1 percent of questions at a cost of 10 cents a miss, the premium would not pay, and RAG would stay.
00a584852b:
The symptom is the wrong clause, not a missing one. That points to chunks that cut and merge clauses and give no way to tell twins apart: faults A and B, at the chunking and enrichment stages.

A larger model reads the same wrong chunk more fluently. A larger k adds more wrong text and spends the prompt budget. Overlap of 40 percent nearly doubles the index and still leaves a fee beside a liability cap in the same chunk.

The fix is structural, and it is cheap: no model call for the title and path. It is measured per contract type because the official bar is per type (95 percent each, 96 overall). Optionally, add a model-written context after the free prefix has been measured.
6a2e56856a:
A prompt instruction is not access control. An output filter acts after the text has been exposed to the model, and it relies on spotting names. Post-filtering the top 10 can leave fewer than k results, or none, for a small tenant. It also only works if the filter is applied everywhere, and a required filter argument plus database row-level security make that structural. Per-customer fine-tuning is expensive, does not solve retrieval, and does not apply to retrieved text.

The correct fix is in the index design. The data to filter on exists on every chunk. The filter is in the query, and it comes from the verified identity. And a test proves it (section 18).
fdf019621e:
"Only small tenants" plus "no errors" is the signature of the selective-filter shortfall (section 19). About 2 percent of candidates belong to a tenant that owns 2 percent of the rows.

Re-chunking and re-embedding would change nothing, because the problem is in the candidate-versus-filter order. Asking for 50 results when the filter removes 98 percent of candidates still leaves one or two rows. The fix is to make the scan continue until the filtered set is full, or to remove the problem by isolating the tenant. Then monitor the symptom.
cd0b4cf22f:
A cache entry becomes readable only after the writing request has completed. So concurrent requests for the same prefix all miss, and each pays the 1.25 times write. That can cost more than not caching (section 14: 4.1 times the sequential run, 1.2 times the uncached run). The diagnostic is the usage counters: creation tokens high, reads near zero.

The other options miss. A larger model raises the cost. Shorter contexts reduce output, not the dominant input term. Moving the document to the user turn does not change caching. What matters is the stable prefix and the cache marker.

The same symptom has other causes: a prefix below the minimum length, a changing prefix, a missing marker (check the docs).
516f570f46:
The feed is the fast path. It cannot be the only path, because events get lost. The guarantee comes from a cheap comparison that bounds the exposure window at the reconciliation cadence. The companion measures 5 minutes, against 12.8 hours for a nightly pass.

Re-indexing everything hourly pays to re-read and re-embed content when only permissions needed checking. A prompt instruction is not access control. Caching permissions for the session lengthens the window instead of shortening it.

Add monitoring for the number of ACL repairs per run. A sudden rise means the feed is broken.
e13715618f:
Embeddings place identifiers that differ by a digit near each other. The companion shows a cosine of 0.64 between two codes one digit apart, and 10 of 12 correct against 12 of 12 for BM25. An exact rare token is what an inverted index is for.

A bigger model may improve it somewhat, but it does not change the nature of the problem. Larger chunks dilute the code. Lowercasing is harmless and does nothing here.

Note the second half of the answer. Adding a second retriever is a change to be measured, since fusion can lower some query kinds (section 16).
54be42c12a: RAG or long context? 9 million tokens exceeds any window. There are per-group restrictions. And the content changes daily. All three hard constraints say RAG (section 4).
427c72a495: Sizing. Pages average 1,450 tokens. At about 400 tokens per chunk that is 22,500 chunks, or 92 MB of 1,024-dimension vectors. One Postgres instance with pgvector and full-text search is ample, and the team already runs Postgres. Engineers search by alarm code and node name, so the lexical index is a requirement, not an option (section 16).
378a0ede96: Chunking. The natural unit is the procedure, so use the procedure mode. Keep a whole procedure (heading and all steps) together up to about 1,200 tokens. Split longer ones on step boundaries, with the title repeated. No fixed overlap. A step out of context ("now restart the AMF pod") is dangerous, so a chunk that starts mid-procedure repeats the procedure's title and says so.
8cc905f56a: Enrichment. Put title and section path in the indexed text. Store network domain, vendor and equipment model as metadata. Take acl_groups from the space and page restrictions, stored as group ids and expanded for the user at query time. Contextual retrieval over the backfill with a small model would cost about 30 dollars (section 14), which is negligible. Still, measure it against the free title-and-path prefix on 200 labelled questions before keeping it for incremental updates.
630be40055: Freshness. Confluence webhooks on page update and restriction change feed a queue. Forty edits a day at about 25 seconds each is 1,000 seconds of work a day, under 0.5 percent of one worker. So a single worker with a one-minute poll gives a lag of about a minute, and the p95 SLO keeps a 9-minute margin for bursts. Permission changes take a separate lane that updates ACLs in seconds, without parsing or embedding.
8cbd94a4a5: Revocation guarantee. A 15-minute ACL-only reconciliation compares page ids and restriction hashes. At an assumed 10 requests per second, 6,200 per-page restriction lookups take 10 minutes, which leaves almost no margin. So use space-level permission listings and "changed since" queries where the source offers them (check the docs for the API), and a pass completes in a minute or two. The nightly full pass compares versions and finds orphans and parser regressions.
356d460d74: Query path. The caller's groups come from the verified token (chapter 7). The retriever filters on tenant, currency and groups, and runs vector and lexical searches (chapter 9 chooses the fusion and any reranker). It fills a budget of about 2,000 tokens. Latency is a budget to measure: query embedding, two index queries, fusion, model generation. If retrieval takes 300 ms and generation 3.5 s, the 6-second p95 has room. On cost, 2,000 chunk tokens plus 1,500 of instructions at an illustrative 3 dollars per million is about $0.011 plus output, under the $0.03 ceiling.
de8ea579c9: Evaluation. Write 200 labelled questions per domain (RAN, core, transport). The bar is recall@10 of at least 0.90 per domain. With 190 of 200 correct, the lower end of a 95 percent interval is about 0.91, and that is what a release gate should compare (chapter 11 on intervals). An ACL test suite runs for every restricted runbook. A query from an unauthorised identity that would otherwise retrieve it must return nothing from it. Zero leaks tolerated.
4b48c44b87: Diagnose before changing anything. Sample 100 wrong-clause answers and classify each by fault (section 3). Here is a plausible split, to be replaced by your own: 61 cut or merged clauses (fault A/B at the chunker), 27 right clause of the wrong customer (fault B, no context), 7 retrieved text the user could not open (fault C), 5 other. The classification orders the work: structure first, then context, then access. Numbers in this paragraph are illustrative.
60ad50ef54: Parsing and sizing. Send native PDFs through a layout-aware extractor. Detect scanned pages (about 128,000 pages) by low character counts and send them to a vision-capable model, for about $770 at illustrative prices (section 7). Have a person check a 100-page sample per route. Clause chunking gives about 2.06 million chunks at 350 tokens, and the vectors take 8.4 GB. That fits on one large Postgres node. But the HNSW build takes hours and needs memory planning, and the filters are selective (a deal team is perhaps 1 percent of the estate). So plan iterative scans or partitions by business unit (section 19).
408964f1b8: Contextual retrieval, measured not assumed. Cost is shape-dependent. At the illustrative prices, 18,000-token contracts in 350-token chunks cost about $8.80 per million document tokens. That is about $6,300 for the estate, or about half with batch processing if its terms allow (check the docs). Run the free title-and-path prefix first. Then run the model-written context on a stratified sample of 600 contracts, 50 per type, and compare. Extend it only to the types where the gain per dollar justifies it.
ec58096035: Labelled set. To show 95 percent per type, you need enough questions per type. Zero failures in 59 questions has a 95 percent lower bound just above 0.95. One failure needs 93 (chapter 1's companion computes this). So plan 100 questions per type, 1,200 in all. At four minutes of lawyer time per question that is 80 hours, the largest cost in the project. Staff it early, and keep the set as the permanent regression suite (chapter 11).
48c0f184fc: Release gate. The gate is a per-type table of clause-citation correctness with intervals, plus overall correctness, the ACL leak test, and p95 latency. Any type below 95 percent blocks launch. The remedy is usually specific to the type: a table-heavy schedule type needs row chunks, and a scanned-heavy type needs a better route.
4cf4bdf6c3: Maintenance. Amendments mark old chunks superseded with an effective date, and the old chunks are kept for "as of" questions. New and changed contracts arrive daily through the feed. A nightly reconciliation compares ids, versions and ACL hashes. Embedding or chunker changes go through the blue/green path with the per-type switching rule (section 22).
4a44565200: Requirement that decides the design. Answers depend on a date that comes from another system (the order), not from the question text. Treat the sale date as a structured parameter that code supplies from the order system. Never let the model infer it. The retrieval filter is effective_from <= as_of AND (effective_to IS NULL OR as_of < effective_to), plus region and product class from the associate's store and the item.
66ab47be11: Versioned chunks without storage blow-up. Keeping every weekly page version means 150 changed pages a week. That is about 7,800 extra page versions a year, or 3.6 times the page count after one year. Version at chunk level instead. When a page changes, only sections whose text hash changed get a new row, and the old row's effective_to is set. Unchanged sections keep their rows. If about 15 percent of a changed page's sections actually change, the year's growth is about 1,170 page-equivalents, roughly 1.4 times the original estate. Section-keyed ids plus a version suffix make this natural.
4be473ce29: Chunking. Chunk structure-aware by section. Each chunk carries title, path, region, product class, effective_from, effective_to and version. Rate and fee tables go in row by row, and price questions that are calculations route to SQL (chapter 9).
c6ff2fca1e: Freshness. Policies go live on a stated date. The pipeline ingests a new version ahead of time with a future effective_from, so no ingest lag can make a policy late. The as-of filter does the switching. Withdrawn policies set effective_to, and they are deleted from the index only after the retention period.
787e7b3c06: Evaluation. Build a date-sensitive test set. For each of 40 policies that changed in the last year, ask questions with sale dates before and after the change, and expect different answers. This tests the filter, which a plain recall test cannot. Add a grounding check that the cited version's date range contains the sale date.
39e3558156: Use the companion folder ccarp-companion/08-rag-pipeline-design/. Everything runs offline with --mock. Four examples import the fake client (07, 08, 14, 17), and they need a Python with the anthropic package. The rest use only the standard library.

3aea22dfce: In 09_acl_prefilter_vs_postfilter.py, add a fifth identity that belongs to core-net but to a different tenant. Add a fourth search path (parent fetch by id) that deliberately skips the filter. Run the leak test and read its failure. Then fix the path.
f18532b576: In 10_filtered_ann_shortfall.py, change the small tenant to 0.5 percent of the rows. How large must ef be for the post-filter strategy to fill 10 rows? What does that do to latency in a real index (estimate from the candidate count)? Which fix would you choose, and why?

Then replace corpus.py's generated documents with 20 to 30 documents from your own work, such as contracts, runbooks or FAQs (remove anything confidential before it touches a shared machine). a208d2dbfb:
Done when:

  • you can size a RAG system from a requirements card (chunks, vector bytes, backfill cost, premium over long context);
  • you can explain from measurements why each of the six decisions in this chapter (parse, chunk, enrich, index both ways, filter inside the query, reconcile) exists;
  • you have seen the ACL leak test fail and pass;
  • you can write the switching rule for a migration before running it.
